Teaser Text 
Assessing job exposure is difficult since reliable evaluation methods are rare and some exposures date 
back to several decades. However, job exposure matrices -JEMs- are simple tools allowing standardized 
assessment of exposure of workers. In this study, we used a JEM to assess occupational silica exposure 
among patients with systemic sclerosis, showing accurate and reliable results, especially to detect 
positive cases. 
What is already known about this subject: Silica is a risk factor for the development of systemic 
sclerosis. Job exposure matrices -JEMs- are interesting tools for occupational exposure assessment for 
epidemiological research.  
What this study adds: JEMs provide reliable results to assess occupational exposure to silica among 
systemic sclerosis patients.  
What impact this may have on practice or policy: JEMs might be a useful and reproductible tool to 
be used in clinical setting and might have possible perspective in term of prevention, compensation, and 
management of occupational disease as well as research. 
 
ABSTRACT 
BACKGROUND: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is the connective tissue disease with the highest individual 
mortality. Crystalline silica is known to be an occupational risk factor for SSc, but exposure may occur 
several decades before disease onset and secondary to several jobs in the patients’ career. To assess past 
crystalline silica exposure, we aimed to study the validity of a job exposure matrix (JEM) to assess 
occupational exposure to crystalline silica compared to specific occupational interviews in two 
populations of SSc patients.  
AIM: To demonstrate the reliability of JEM for the assessment of occupational exposure to hazards 
such as silica, in severe rare disorders like SSc. 
METHOD:  Patients from two university hospital centres underwent standardized assessment of 
occupational silica exposure and collected job histories through face to face interviews. A JEM from the 
French program Matgéné was used to assess silica exposure and compared to the standardized interview 
results. Standard metrics were computed for evaluate the accuracy of JEM. 
RESULTS: 67 participants from Rennes, and 119 from Tours were included, with respectively 10.5% 
and 18.0% of patients with silica exposure based on the results of the interview. The JEM with 50% 
probability cut-off had a good performance when compared with the classic assessment method. A 
cumulative exposure index from JEM over 250 had an AUC between 0.76 and 0.79 and also a very high 
positive likelihood ratio (17.14 and 10.29). 
CONCLUSION: Despite limitations inherent to JEMs and associated validation methods, the JEM used 
in this setting provided accurate results to assess occupational exposure to crystalline silica for clinical 
purposes such as in SSc patients, especially to detect positive cases. These results offer new perspectives 
in terms of prevention, compensation, and management of occupational diseases as well as research. 
KEY WORDS: Occupational exposure; Silica; Job Exposure Matrix; Validity; Accuracy; Systemic 
sclerosis.

Introduction 
Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is the connective tissue disease with the highest individual mortality, mainly 
due to fibrotic interstitial lung disease. Current treatment options rely on immunomodulatory therapies 
although disease modifying therapy are still needed.(1,2)  
There is now evidence that some environmental factors are directly linked to SSc onset, include exposure 
to inhaled crystalline silica (SiO2).(3–5) SiO2 impacts lung function decline over time in SSc.(6) In USA 
about 2.3 million workers are exposed to SiO2.(7) However, retrospective assessment of SiO2 in 
workplace remains challenging, often requiring time-consuming and costly standardized interviews by 
trained specialists.  
Several alternative tools are available to overcome such issues, including job-exposure matrices (JEMs). 
JEMs provide a global assessment exposure to specific hazards by cross-referencing job titles and sector 
of activity.(8,9) JEMs are based on direct measures, self-reported exposure and/or expert assessment 
and offer exposure measurements including frequency/intensity/probability of exposure. These data are 
often adapted according to the period and duration of the job. 
Some JEMs have demonstrated their usefulness not only for epidemiological purposes but also for 
individual risk assessment, although there are still only few studies available and further research is 
needed, especially for SiO2 exposure and associated-health outcomes.(10,11)  
This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of a JEM for measuring occupational exposure to SiO2 in 
populations of patients with SSc from two independent centres. 
 
Methods 
Two population of patients with SSc from two French university centres (Rennes and Tours) who 
fulfilled the 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria were consecutively included.(12) All patients were 
prospectively interviewed about their occupational exposure to SiO2 from 2013 to 2015 in Rennes, and 
from 1999 to 2018, in Tours. Patients with missing data from both centers were not included.  
The reference assessment method for SiO2 exposure was a face-to-face standardized interview 
administered by internal medicine physicians trained by occupational practitioners. This interview 
included a full job history and details of potential occupational risk asked for each job period with 
exposure (supplemental 1). Participants were considered exposed to SiO2 at work if they reported SiO2 
exposure for at least one year in their working life.  
The JEM used in this study originates from the “Matgéné program”.(13,14) This JEM have different 
exposure including silica. For Silica JEM, for each combination of job, activities and time period, a 
value of frequency, intensity and probability of silica exposure is given. Thus, based on work exposure 
assessed by previous interview, jobs were blindly and independently coded in the French Job Coding 
system using the CAPS tool (“Codage Assisté des Professions et Secteurs d'activité”).(15) Probability 
of exposure from JEM were considered at four thresholds (20%, 50%, 70% and 90%).  Using the 
interview as reference, sensitivity/specificity/positive-negative predictive values, likelihood ratios for 
positive (LR+) and negative testing (LR-) were calculated for each four thresholds of the JEMs in the 
Rennes and Tours SSc populations separately. A cumulative exposure index (CEI) was also calculated 
as follow: CEI=frequency*intensity*probability*length for the JEM as recommended by its authors. 
Area Under the Curve (AUCs) provided by Receiver Operating Characteristics curve were calculated. 
The optimal cut-off value for CEI was identified using Youden statistic. The cut-offs determined in 
Tours and Rennes populations were switched and applied to the other population to check stability of 
the thresholds. 


All patients gave written consent and the study obtained approval from the local ethics committee 
(“Comité éthique CHU de Rennes” n14-53 and “Espace de Réflexion Ethique Région Centre” n2018-
096). Analyses were conducted using R (v4.2.1, “pROC” package) and STATA v17.0SE.  
Results 
Among the 250 eligible patients that were interviewed in Rennes and Tours, 57 were excluded from 
Rennes due to a different assessment approach as compared to interview from Tours and 7 for missing 
data regarding occupational activities and/or sector of activity. In total, 186 were included, 67 from 
Rennes and 119 from Tours. For Rennes, there were 52 women (77.5%). According to the interview, 7 
were exposed to SiO2 (10.5%). For Tours, there was 68 women (66.5%) with 18 were exposed (18%) 
to SiO2 according to the face-to-face standardized interviews.  
The French JEM had high specificity and LR+ at 50% threshold, with an acceptable sensitivity and LR- 
(Table 1). Results were similar using the CEI, with an AUC at 0.77 and 0.79 (figure 1). The similar 
accuracy results between the two centres, the similar threshold for 50% probability and threshold at 250 
(range between 216 and 270), allowed the definition of a cut-off value at 250 with good external validity.  
 
Discussion 
The SiO2 JEM had good performances among SSc patients. Results were consistent using a 50% 
probability exposure as threshold or a 250 CEI score, with similar results between the two independent 
centres.  
Although JEMs have been for screening of exposure to asbestos and SiO2 in patients with lung 
cancer,(16) there was no application in independent populations of SSc patients and/or in multicenter 
studies in rare autoimmune occupational diseases. Results for SiO2 exposure in SSc are similar to those 
of lung cancer with a good positive predictive value (8.17 [3.8–10]), increasing the external validity of 
the Matgéné JEM when applied in these disorders. Matgéné was also used to assess occupational 
exposure to organic solvents, showing consistent association with pulmonary veno-occlusive disease as 
compared to a standardised questionnaire in a previous study from our group.(17) 
Limitations of our study include the overall exposure estimation by JEMs, which reflect an "average" 
level of exposures and cannot account for exposure heterogeneity due to individual contextual 
specificities.(18) Furthermore, JEM is based on evaluations made by experts when they build the 
algorithm, and working conditions continually evolve, with updates need to be discussed. Coding 
job/sector might also represent a limitation, explaining why a blind coding was performed. Having only 
limited number of patients/centre lead to large confidence intervals, although such sample size were 
expected for a rare disease. The similar performance of JEM within the two independent populations 
are also promising, strengthening the consistency of our findings. Using interview as the reference might 
also underestimate the exposure, although no other standard exists in such retrospective assessment for 
systemic autoimmune diseases.(19) 
The use of JEMs as assessment tool for occupational exposure associated with chronic diseases might 
allow reliable occupational assessment when no occupational practitioners are available, participating 
in the optimisation of future prevention strategies. It could also help patients obtain financial 
compensations depending on the compensation system. As they allow reliable latency and temporal 
analyses, JEMs could also be especially relevant for research purposes in the field of other rare diseases 
with potential SiO2 exposure like Rheumatoid Arthritis or Systemic Lupus, or unknown aetiologies, such 
as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Abstract: BACKGROUND: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is the connective tissue disease with the highest individual mortality. Crystalline silica is known to be an occupational risk factor for SSc, but exposure may occur several decades before disease onset and secondary to several jobs in the patients’ career. To assess past crystalline silica exposure, we aimed to study the validity of a job exposure matrix (JEM) to assess occupational exposure to crystalline silica compared to specific occupational interviews in two populations of SSc patients. AIM: To demonstrate the reliability of JEM for the assessment of occupational exposure to hazards such as silica, in severe rare disorders like SSc. METHOD: Patients from two university hospital centres underwent standardized assessment of occupational silica exposure and collected job histories through face to face interviews. A JEM from the French program Matgéné was used to assess silica exposure and compared to the standardized interview results. Standard metrics were computed for evaluate the accuracy of JEM. RESULTS: 67 participants from Rennes, and 119 from Tours were included, with respectively 10.5% and 18.0% of patients with silica exposure based on the results of the interview. The JEM with 50% probability cut-off had a good performance when compared with the classic assessment method. A cumulative exposure index from JEM over 250 had an AUC between 0.76 and 0.79 and also a very high positive likelihood ratio (17.14 and 10.29). CONCLUSION: Despite limitations inherent to JEMs and associated validation methods, the JEM used in this setting provided accurate results to assess occupational exposure to crystalline silica for clinical purposes such as in SSc patients, especially to detect positive cases. These results offer new perspectives in terms of prevention, compensation, and management of occupational diseases as well as research.
